claim: Monocytes are phagocytic effector cells in the blood and precursors of resident and inflammatory tissue macrophages.
source: Monocytes are phagocytic effector cells in the blood and precursors of resident and inflammatory tissue macrophages.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about monocyte function and differentiation.

claim: ECFP and EGFP transgenic reporters based upon Csf1r and Cx3cr1 distinguish monocytes from resident mononuclear phagocytes.
source: ECFP and EGFP transgenic reporters based upon Csf1r and Cx3cr1 distinguish monocytes from resident mononuclear phagocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript using these transgenic reporter systems.

claim: Migratory monocytes were found to be either patrolling within large vessels of the lung or locating at the interface between lung capillaries and alveoli.
source: Migratory monocytes were found to be either patrolling within large vessels of the lung or locating at the interface between lung capillaries and alveoli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Monocytes have the property to capture fluorescent particles derived from both vascular and airway routes.
source: This spatial organisation gives to monocytes the property to capture fluorescent particles derived from both vascular and airway routes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing particle uptake from both routes.

claim: Monocytes participate in steady-state surveillance of the lung without differentiating into macrophages.
source: We conclude that monocytes participate in steady-state surveillance of the lung, in a way that is complementary to resident macrophages and DC, without differentiating into macrophages.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by parabiosis experiments and imaging data showing monocyte behavior.

claim: The lung is a mucosal surface of the body, exposed constantly to inhaled particles including pathogens, as well as other potential toxins.
source: The lung is a mucosal surface of the body, exposed constantly to inhaled particles including pathogens, as well as other potential toxins (Nelson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Lung mononuclear phagocytes have been shown to adapt specifically to the lung environment, and contribute to lung homeostasis, scavenging, and immune surveillance.
source: Lung mononuclear phagocytes have been shown to adapt specifically to the lung environment, and contribute to lung homeostasis, scavenging, and immune surveillance (Kopf et al., 2014; The lungs at the frontlines of immunity, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Monocytes were originally considered to be circulating precursors of macrophages, participating in renewal of tissue-resident macrophages in steady state and recruited in large numbers in response to inflammatory stimuli.
source: Monocytes were originally considered to be circulating precursors of macrophages, participating in renewal of tissue-resident macrophages in steady state and recruited in large numbers in response to inflammatory stimuli (Auffray et al., 2009; Geissmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Fate mapping approaches and parabiosis experiments have been used to argue that tissue-resident macrophages such as alveolar macrophages may be seeded from the yolk sac or foetal liver during embryonic development and can be maintained in the absence of monocyte recruitment.
source: Fate mapping approaches and parabiosis experiments have been used to argue that tissue-resident macrophages such as alveolar macrophages (AM) may be seeded from the yolk sac or foetal liver during embryonic development and can be maintained in the absence of monocyte recruitment (Guilliams et al., 2013; Hashimoto et al., 2013; Yona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Monocytes derived from the bone marrow and spleen can replenish tissue macrophages after their cytotoxic depletion.
source: Whatever their normal contribution to the resident macrophage pool, monocytes derived from the bone marrow (Chow et al., 2011) and spleen (Swirski et al., 2009) can clearly replenish tissue macrophages after their cytotoxic depletion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Monocytes carry out specific effector functions during infection.
source: Beyond this precursor role, monocytes carry out specific effector functions during infection (Serbina et al., 2008) and may be involved in steady-state tissue surveillance by capturing and transporting antigen from tissue to lymphoid organs (Jakubzick et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Monocytes may be involved in steady-state tissue surveillance by capturing and transporting antigen from tissue to lymphoid organs.
source: Beyond this precursor role, monocytes carry out specific effector functions during infection (Serbina et al., 2008) and may be involved in steady-state tissue surveillance by capturing and transporting antigen from tissue to lymphoid organs (Jakubzick et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Macrophages isolated from different organs have distinct expression profiles which can be distinguished further if the cells are separated according to their surface markers.
source: Macrophages isolated from different organs have distinct expression profiles which can be distinguished further if the cells are separated according to their surface markers (Gautier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: No available surface marker is well correlated with any other marker, at either the protein or mRNA level.
source: Unfortunately, no available surface marker is well correlated with any other marker, at either the protein or mRNA level (Hume, 2008, 2012; Hume et al., 2010), so the number of macrophage subsets definable by flow cytometry is essentially infinite (Becher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The number of macrophage subsets definable by flow cytometry is essentially infinite.
source: Unfortunately, no available surface marker is well correlated with any other marker, at either the protein or mRNA level (Hume, 2008, 2012; Hume et al., 2010), so the number of macrophage subsets definable by flow cytometry is essentially infinite (Becher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: Classical monocytes express high levels of both Ly6C and the chemokine receptor CCR2 but a low level of the fractalkine (CX3CL1) receptor CX3CR1.
source: In the mouse, one subset called classical monocytes, expresses high levels of both Ly6C and the chemokine receptor CCR2 but a low level of the fractalkine (CX3CL1) receptor CX3CR1, while the second, the so-called non-classical monocytes, lacks Ly6C but expresses a high level of CX3CR1 (Geissmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Non-classical monocytes lack Ly6C but express a high level of CX3CR1.
source: In the mouse, one subset called classical monocytes, expresses high levels of both Ly6C and the chemokine receptor CCR2 but a low level of the fractalkine (CX3CL1) receptor CX3CR1, while the second, the so-called non-classical monocytes, lacks Ly6C but expresses a high level of CX3CR1 (Geissmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A Csf1r-EGFP reporter gene serves as a definitive marker of MPS cells.
source: A Csf1r-EGFP reporter gene serves as a definitive marker of MPS cells (Sasmono et al., 2003), while a Cx3cr1-EGFP reporter labels the non-classical monocytes as well as subsets of tissue macrophages, including microglia, as well as a subset of natural killer (NK) lymphocytes (Jung et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A Cx3cr1-EGFP reporter labels the non-classical monocytes as well as subsets of tissue macrophages, including microglia, as well as a subset of natural killer (NK) lymphocytes.
source: A Csf1r-EGFP reporter gene serves as a definitive marker of MPS cells (Sasmono et al., 2003), while a Cx3cr1-EGFP reporter labels the non-classical monocytes as well as subsets of tissue macrophages, including microglia, as well as a subset of natural killer (NK) lymphocytes (Jung et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Itgax-YFP transgenic mouse was considered to provide a marker for classical 'dendritic cells'.
source: The Itgax-YFP transgenic mouse was considered to provide a marker for classical 'dendritic cells' (Lindquist et al., 2004) and has been used to image so-called interstitial DC in the lung (Looney et al., 2011; Thornton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Itgax-YFP reporter is rather uniformly expressed in tissue macrophages associated with mucosa and in the lung provides a generic MPS marker.
source: However, this reporter is rather uniformly expressed in tissue macrophages associated with mucosa and in the lung provides a generic MPS marker (Hume, 2008, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The deletion of a conserved distal element of the Csf1r promoter in the Csf1r-ECFPtg/+ mouse (MacBlue) ablates expression of a reporter gene in trophoblasts, osteoclasts, granulocytes, and many tissue macrophages.
source: The deletion of a conserved distal element of the Csf1r promoter in the Csf1r-ECFPtg/+ mouse (MacBlue) ablates expression of a reporter gene in trophoblasts, osteoclasts, granulocytes, and many tissue macrophages (Ovchinnikov et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: All blood monocytes in MacBlue mice are strongly ECFP+, whereas most tissue macrophages do not express the reporter protein.
source: All blood monocytes in these MacBlue mice are strongly ECFP+, whereas most tissue macrophages do not express the reporter protein (Sauter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Stellar EGFP+ECFPneg cells were seen in the collagen membrane surrounding the lung pleura.
source: Stellar EGFP+ECFPneg cells were seen in the collagen membrane surrounding the lung pleura (Figure 1A,B, green squares), deeper in the lung parenchyma with small round shapes or stellar shapes (Figure 1B, green squares), and along the basal membranes of bronchial airways (Figure 1C, green squares).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Stellar EGFP+ECFPneg cells were seen deeper in the lung parenchyma with small round shapes or stellar shapes.
source: Stellar EGFP+ECFPneg cells were seen in the collagen membrane surrounding the lung pleura (Figure 1A,B, green squares), deeper in the lung parenchyma with small round shapes or stellar shapes (Figure 1B, green squares), and along the basal membranes of bronchial airways (Figure 1C, green squares).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Stellar EGFP+ECFPneg cells were seen along the basal membranes of bronchial airways.
source: Stellar EGFP+ECFPneg cells were seen in the collagen membrane surrounding the lung pleura (Figure 1A,B, green squares), deeper in the lung parenchyma with small round shapes or stellar shapes (Figure 1B, green squares), and along the basal membranes of bronchial airways (Figure 1C, green squares).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The luminal side of airways and alveoli contained large round ECFP+ cells, likely AM.
source: The luminal side of airways and alveoli contained large round ECFP+ cells, likely AM (Figure 1A–D, pink squares).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Smaller amoeboid-like ECFP+ cells were located in the interstitial space of the lung parenchyma.
source: Smaller amoeboid-like ECFP+ cells were located in the interstitial space of the lung parenchyma (Figure 1A–D, purple squares).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The MacBlue ECFP transgene was expressed only in AM and monocyte-like cells, whereas most interstitial CX3CR1-EGFP expressing cells lacked expression.
source: In overview, the pattern was consistent with previous evidence that the MacBlue ECFP transgene was expressed only in AM and monocyte-like cells, whereas most interstitial CX3CR1-EGFP expressing cells lacked expression.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data and previous evidence.

claim: The CX3CR1-EGFPlow population was Ly6ChighCD11b+Ly6GnegF4/80intNK1.1negCD64+ in both the blood and the lungs, consistent with identity as 'classical' Ly6Chigh monocytes.
source: The CX3CR1-EGFPlow population was Ly6ChighCD11b+Ly6GnegF4/80intNK1.1negCD64+ (blue gate) in both the blood and the lungs (Table 1), consistent with identity as 'classical' Ly6Chigh monocytes (Ly6Chigh Mo).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The CX3CR1-EGFPhigh population was Ly6ClowCD11b+Ly6GnegF4/80intNK1.1negCD64+CD11c+ phenotype, consistent with the phenotype of the Ly6Clow monocyte subset.
source: The CX3CR1-EGFPhigh population was Ly6ClowCD11b+Ly6GnegF4/80intNK1.1negCD64+CD11c+ phenotype (red gate), consistent with the phenotype of the Ly6Clow monocyte subset (Ly6Clow Mo) (Guilliams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2 and a citation.

claim: For both monocyte subsets, the expression of CD115 and CD62L was down modulated in the lung cells compared to their circulating counterparts.
source: For both subsets, the expression of CD115 and CD62L was down modulated in the lung cells compared to their circulating counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data comparing blood and lung monocytes.

claim: Downregulation of surface CSF1R (CD115) could reflect the down-modulation of the surface receptor both by its ligand and by the many inflammatory stimuli present in the lung.
source: Downregulation of surface CSF1R (CD115) could reflect the down-modulation of the surface receptor both by its ligand and by the many inflammatory stimuli present in the lung (Sester et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: The lung contained an ECFPhighEGFPneg signature that were larger than monocytes and CD11b+Ly6CnegLy6GnegF4/80highNK1.1negCD11chighCD64highSiglecFhigh cells, consistent with their identity as AM.
source: As expected, the lung also contained an ECFPhighEGFPneg signature (pink gate). These cells were larger than monocytes and CD11b+Ly6CnegLy6GnegF4/80highNK1.1negCD11chighCD64highSiglecFhigh cells, consistent with their identity as AM.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In parabionts of MacBlue×Cx3cr1gfp/+ with C57Bl6 mice, donor-derived ECFP cells displayed Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow monocyte phenotypes.
source: In the lung, donor-derived ECFP cells displayed Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow monocyte phenotypes (Figure 3A), were small in size, with ameboid-like morphologies, and were all located in the interalveolar space (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In parabionts, donor-derived ECFP cells were small in size, with ameboid-like morphologies, and were all located in the interalveolar space.
source: In the lung, donor-derived ECFP cells displayed Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow monocyte phenotypes (Figure 3A), were small in size, with ameboid-like morphologies, and were all located in the interalveolar space (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neither AM nor interstitial macrophages were derived from the donor in parabiosis experiments as there was no expression of the transgenes in these compartments.
source: By contrast, neither AM nor interstitial macrophages were derived from the donor as there was no expression of the transgenes in these compartments (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The only cells expressing EGFP but not ECFP in parabionts were NK cells derived from the donor.
source: The only cells expressing EGFP but not ECFP, were NK cells derived from the donor (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The frequency of circulating Ly6Chigh monocytes was similar in wild-type and Cx3cr1−/− mice.
source: Consistent with published studies (Kim et al., 2011; Yona et al., 2013), the frequency of circulating Ly6Chigh monocytes was similar in wild-type (WT) and Cx3cr1−/− mice.
evidence: This is supported by data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The absence of CX3CR1 did impact on the yield of Ly6Chigh cells in the lung.
source: By contrast, the absence of CX3CR1 did impact on the yield of Ly6Chigh cells in the lung.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and Cx3cr1−/− mice.

claim: Ly6Chigh monocytes were strongly reduced in Ccr2−/− mice and dKO mice in both the blood and the lungs.
source: As expected, this subset was strongly reduced in Ccr2−/− mice and dKO mice in both the blood and the lungs (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ly6Clow monocyte frequency was similar in Ccr2−/− mice but significantly reduced in Cx3cr1−/− and dKO mice in both the blood and the lungs compared to WT mice.
source: Ly6Clow monocyte frequency was similar in Ccr2−/− mice but significantly reduced in Cx3cr1−/− and dKO mice in both the blood and the lungs compared to WT mice (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: AM frequencies were similar in all strains consistent with their reported monocyte-independent homeostasis.
source: AM frequencies were similar in all strains (Figure 4C) consistent with their reported monocyte-independent homeostasis (Guilliams et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and a citation.

claim: CCR2 and CX3CR1 control the steady-state trafficking and survival of both Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow monocyte-derived cells in the lungs.
source: Together, these results showed that CCR2 and CX3CR1 control the steady-state trafficking and survival of both Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow monocyte-derived cells in the lungs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing different knockout mice.

claim: Small interstitial ECFP+ cells (area 61 ± 17 μm²) with an amoeboid-like shape displayed a bimodal behaviour: they were either highly motile, going backwards and forwards between the alveoli, or relatively sessile with protrusions extending towards the lumen of the alveoli.
source: Small interstitial ECFP+ cells (area 61 ± 17 μm²) with an amoeboid-like shape displayed a bimodal behaviour: they were either highly motile, going backwards and forwards between the alveoli, or relatively sessile with protrusions extending towards the lumen of the alveoli (Figure 5B–C and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5 and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Patrolling cells have high velocity (10 ± 4.6 μm/min) and a low arrest coefficient (14 ± 13%).
source: Based upon these distinct behaviours, we defined 'patrolling' cells with high velocity (10 ± 4.6 μm/min) and a low arrest coefficient (14 ± 13%) and interstitial ECFP+ cells with lower velocity (4 ± 2.2 μm/min) and a higher arrest coefficient (64 ± 21%) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Interstitial ECFP+ cells have lower velocity (4 ± 2.2 μm/min) and a higher arrest coefficient (64 ± 21%).
source: Based upon these distinct behaviours, we defined 'patrolling' cells with high velocity (10 ± 4.6 μm/min) and a low arrest coefficient (14 ± 13%) and interstitial ECFP+ cells with lower velocity (4 ± 2.2 μm/min) and a higher arrest coefficient (64 ± 21%) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fast moving patrolling ECFP+ cells were located inside large vessels, whereas slow motile ECFP+ cells appeared to be extravascular but in close contact with the vasculature.
source: Intravenous injection of rhodamine dextran prior to mouse sacrifice permitted, during a short time frame before vascular leakage, to determine that fast moving patrolling ECFP+ cells were located inside large vessels, whereas slow motile ECFP+ cells appeared to be extravascular but in close contact with the vasculature (Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Video 3.

claim: Large round ECFPbright AM (area 121 ± 23 μm²) were detected in the alveolar lumina, leisurely surveying the surface of the airways with a velocity of 2 ± 1.5 μm/min and a high arrest coefficient (76 ± 19%).
source: Aside from monocytes, large round ECFPbright AM (area 121 ± 23 μm²) were detected in the alveolar lumina, leisurely surveying the surface of the airways with a velocity of 2 ± 1.5 μm/min and a high arrest coefficient (76 ± 19%) (Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Video 4.

claim: Interstitial EGFP+ cells migrated slowly, with comparable velocity and arrest coefficient to AM.
source: Interstitial EGFP+ cells also migrated slowly, with comparable velocity and arrest coefficient to AM (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The MC of patrolling monocytes was 30-fold higher than the MC of interstitial ECFP+ cells (39 vs 1.3 μm²/min) and a further fourfold higher than the MC of AM (0.3 μm²/min).
source: The MC of patrolling monocytes was 30-fold higher than the MC of interstitial ECFP+ cells (39 vs 1.3 μm²/min) and a further fourfold higher than the MC of AM (0.3 μm²/min) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The higher MC in interstitial ECFP+ monocytes was attributable to the protrusive activity and slow displacement suggesting scanning of the interalveolar space.
source: This higher MC in interstitial ECFP+ monocytes was attributable to the protrusive activity and slow displacement suggesting scanning of the interalveolar space (Video 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data shown in Video 2.

claim: While AM survey the luminal side of the alveoli, interstitial monocyte-derived cells survey the lung tissue through either active patrolling in the vasculature or protrusive activity toward the alveolar space.
source: In overview, while AM survey the luminal side of the alveoli, interstitial monocyte-derived cells survey the lung tissue through either active patrolling in the vasculature or protrusive activity toward the alveolar space.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the imaging data.

claim: The absence of functional CX3CR1 did not change the arrest coefficient of patrolling cells.
source: The absence of functional CX3CR1 did not change the arrest coefficient (Figure 6B) but did slightly reduce the MC of patrolling cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The absence of functional CX3CR1 did slightly reduce the MC of patrolling cells.
source: The absence of functional CX3CR1 did not change the arrest coefficient (Figure 6B) but did slightly reduce the MC of patrolling cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: AM behaviour was comparable in WT and Cx3cr1−/− mice.
source: As might be anticipated given their lack of CX3CR1 expression, AM behaviour was also comparable in WT and Cx3cr1−/− mice (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Deletion of the CX3CR1 clearly altered the behaviour of the interstitial ECFP+ cells, which showed a greatly increased arrest coefficient and reduced MC.
source: On the other hand, deletion of the CX3CR1 clearly altered the behaviour of the interstitial ECFP+ cells, which showed a greatly increased arrest coefficient and reduced MC (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the absence of CX3CR1, the remaining interstitial ECFP+ cells present had greatly reduced protrusive activity, as indicated by increased global 'sphericity' and reduced sphericity variation.
source: In the absence of CX3CR1, the remaining interstitial ECFP+ cells present had greatly reduced protrusive activity, as indicated by increased global 'sphericity' (Figure 6D,E) and reduced sphericity variation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: YFP expression was mainly restricted to the defined classical DC subsets with a brighter expression for CD11b− DC.
source: Although CD11c mRNA and surface protein are expressed widely among tissue macrophages in the lung, YFP expression was mainly restricted to the defined classical DC subsets with a brighter expression for CD11b− DC (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: AM only express the MacBlue transgene and despite expression of CD11c protein on their surface, YFP was detectable in only a small subset.
source: Interestingly, AM only express the MacBlue transgene and despite expression of CD11c protein on their surface, YFP was detectable in only a small subset (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: AM represented the most abundant mononuclear phagocyte subset of the lung.
source: AM represented the most abundant mononuclear phagocyte subset of the lung (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Lung monocytes represented the second main mononuclear phagocyte subset and were even more numerous than interstitial macrophages, CD11b+ DC and CD11b−CD103+ DC.
source: Lung monocytes represented the second main mononuclear phagocyte subset and were even more numerous than interstitial macrophages, CD11b+ DC and CD11b−CD103+ DC (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7.

claim: YFPbright cells were mainly located along bronchial airways and poorly distributed in the alveolar space in contrast to ECFP+ monocytes and AM.
source: Histological analysis of a lung section of MacBlue×Itgax-YFP showed that YFPbright cells were mainly located along bronchial airways and poorly distributed in the alveolar space in contrast to ECFP+ monocytes and AM (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by histological imaging data shown in Figure 7.

claim: After i.v. inoculation, only monocytic cells appeared to have taken up particles.
source: After i.v. inoculation, only monocytic cells appeared to have taken up particles (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: After airway inhalation, AM were the main phagocytic subset.
source: After airway inhalation, AM were the main phagocytic subset (Figure 8B–C), but particles were also detected among interstitial cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: After airway inhalation, particles were also detected among interstitial cells.
source: After airway inhalation, AM were the main phagocytic subset (Figure 8B–C), but particles were also detected among interstitial cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The numbers of phagocytic Ly6Clow and Ly6Chigh monocytes were significantly higher compared to the number of phagocytic DC after airway inhalation.
source: The numbers of phagocytic Ly6Clow and Ly6Chigh monocytes were significantly higher compared to the number of phagocytic DC after airway inhalation, showing that lung monocytes are the only subsets that effectively capture both blood-derived and airway-derived fluorescent particles (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Lung monocytes are the only subsets that effectively capture both blood-derived and airway-derived fluorescent particles.
source: The numbers of phagocytic Ly6Clow and Ly6Chigh monocytes were significantly higher compared to the number of phagocytic DC after airway inhalation, showing that lung monocytes are the only subsets that effectively capture both blood-derived and airway-derived fluorescent particles (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: AM were not labelled by in vivo CD45 antibody, confirming that the antibody did not reach the airways.
source: AM were not labelled, confirming that the antibody did not reach the airways.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo CD45 labelling data.

claim: 27% of interstitial macrophages, 12% of CD11b+ DC, and only 1% of CD11b− DC were labelled by in vivo CD45 antibody, suggesting a distinct location of these subsets related to the vasculature.
source: Overall, 27% of interstitial macrophages, 12% of CD11b+ DC, and only 1% of CD11b− DC were labelled, suggesting a distinct location of these subsets related to the vasculature (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo CD45 labelling data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Up to 90% of Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow lung monocytes were labelled by the anti-CD45 antibody in vivo; however, the MFI was significantly lower compared to that of blood monocytes.
source: Up to 90% of Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow lung monocytes were labelled by the anti-CD45 antibody in vivo; however, the MFI was significantly lower compared to that of blood monocytes (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo CD45 labelling data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Lung monocytes displayed reduced expression of Ly6C, CD62L, and CD115 compared to circulating monocytes, in addition to a higher level of CD11b.
source: Furthermore, the phenotype of both Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow monocytes was slightly distinct from their circulating counterparts. Indeed lung monocytes displayed reduced expression of Ly6C, CD62L, and CD115 as previously observed, in addition to a higher level of CD11b, whereas only Ly6Clow monocytes displayed higher CD11c expression (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Only Ly6Clow monocytes displayed higher CD11c expression compared to circulating monocytes.
source: Furthermore, the phenotype of both Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow monocytes was slightly distinct from their circulating counterparts. Indeed lung monocytes displayed reduced expression of Ly6C, CD62L, and CD115 as previously observed, in addition to a higher level of CD11b, whereas only Ly6Clow monocytes displayed higher CD11c expression (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Monocytes can be either extravascular but in close vicinity to the vessels or still intravascular and trapped in capillaries with reduced access to the bloodstream and submitted to the lung environment.
source: These results suggest that monocytes can be either extravascular but in close vicinity to the vessels or still intravascular and trapped in capillaries with reduced access to the bloodstream and submitted to the lung environment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the in vivo CD45 labelling data.

claim: In large vessels, ECFP+ cells were mainly round shaped, whereas in the vicinity of capillaries, interstitial ECFP+ cells displayed an elongated or amoeboid-like shape.
source: In large vessels, ECFP+ cells were mainly round shaped, whereas in the vicinity of capillaries, interstitial ECFP+ cells displayed an elongated or amoeboid-like shape (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Interstitial ECFP+ cells locate at the interface between the capillaries and the alveoli either intra- or extravascularly.
source: Confocal analysis of the microvascular area using CD31 staining showed that interstitial ECFP+ cells locate at the interface between the capillaries and the alveoli either intra- or extravascularly (Figure 9E and Video 8).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 9 and Video 8.

claim: CD45 in vivo labelling was exactly the same for both Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow monocytes that had captured the beads compared to non-phagocytic monocytes.
source: CD45 in vivo labelling was exactly the same for both Ly6Chigh and Ly6Clow monocytes that had captured the beads compared to non-phagocytic monocytes (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Lung monocytes are strategically positioned at the interface between the bloodstream and airways to survey both compartments.
source: This result confirmed that lung monocytes are strategically positioned at the interface between the bloodstream and airways to survey both compartments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The MacBlue binary transgene provides a unique marker of blood monocytes.
source: The MacBlue binary transgene (Csf1r-gal4VP16/UAS-ECFP) provides a unique marker of blood monocytes (Jenkins and Hume, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The MacBlue binary transgene, based upon a deleted Csf1r promoter, produced a transgenic line in which the reporter gene is extinguished in the majority of mature tissue macrophages and greatly reduced in granulocytes.
source: The MacBlue binary transgene, based upon a deleted Csf1r promoter, produced a transgenic line in which the reporter gene is extinguished in the majority of mature tissue macrophages and greatly reduced in granulocytes (Ovchinnikov et al., 2008; Sauter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ECFP expression provides a unique marker of cells that have recently derived from monocytes.
source: Despite the fact that ECFP expression is not directly related to the level of Csf1r mRNA, it provides a unique marker of cells that have recently derived from monocytes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MacBlue transgene properties.

claim: The dual reporter avoids potential artefacts created by the γc-deficient background excluding NK cells which are highly represented in the CX3CR1-GFP+ fraction within the lungs.
source: The dual reporter also avoids potential artefacts created by the γc-deficient background excluding NK cells which we have shown to be highly represented in the CX3CR1-GFP+ fraction within the lungs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the advantages of the dual reporter system.
